title: Key created mid-incident has already been used
why: The attacker switched to their own key. Revoking the original key achieves nothing.

title: IAM persistence in the account
why: Independent access that survives revoking the original key. Until it is cleaned up, the account is compromised.

title: Anti-forensics (logging/detection tampering)
why: Deliberate covering of tracks. Anything that happened after this may not have been logged.

title: Access to secrets and credentials
why: If these succeeded, the compromise extends beyond AWS. Treat everything stored there as leaked.

title: Bedrock / ML abuse (LLMjacking)
why: Resale of model access. The bill grows fast and quietly, and no resources show up in the console.

title: Compute launches (cryptomining)
why: The main driver of the bill. Check instance types and regions in the detail column.

title: Mail/messaging abuse (SES/SNS)
why: Spam/phishing sent in the company's name. Beyond the money, this hurts domain reputation and can get it blocklisted.

title: Web console sign-in
why: If the sign-in succeeded, the attacker had a password or a federation token, not just an API key.

title: Bedrock calls
why: Any Bedrock activity on a compromised key is abuse until proven otherwise.

title: Activity spread across 5 regions
why: Fanning out across regions is a signature of automated abuse. A region-restricting SCP cuts it off.

title: Mass permission denials (permission brute-forcing)
why: Looks like automated probing of available APIs. The attempted calls show what they were after.

title: Non-interactive clients (scripts, not console/CLI)
why: This User-Agent does not come from normal work by the company's people or services.

title: Quota increase requests
why: Asking for higher limits means they hit the ceiling and wanted to burn more.

title: Network and access changes
why: Look for 0.0.0.0/0 and for peering into foreign VPCs.

title: Environment reconnaissance
why: Initial reconnaissance. Its makeup identifies the tool, and its timing establishes T0.
